idiom_name: RSpec describe/it example groups with before(:example) hooks and let
implementation_notes: Example groups (describe/context) hold it blocks whose body contains the act and assert beats, while before(:example) hooks and lazy let definitions build the arrange beat per example and expect(...).to matchers carry the assertion. The classic Testcase Class is replaced by the nested group tree; the common one-behaviour-per-example style maps cleanly to AAA, but RSpec does not enforce one act or one expectation. Memoized helpers keep fixtures independent because each example re-evaluates them.
code_sketch:
RSpec.describe Account do
  subject(:account) { described_class.new(balance: 100) }   # Arrange (lazy)

  it 'reduces the balance when 30 is withdrawn' do
    ok = account.withdraw(30)                               # Act
    expect(ok).to be(true)                                  # Assert
    expect(account.balance).to eq(70)
  end
end
pitfalls: let is memoized per example: a spec that mutates the subject changes it for the rest of that example, and a spec that never references the subject never runs its arrange code.
Instance variables assigned in before(:context) are not rolled back between examples - the RSpec docs warn about sharing state there - which quietly couples examples.
A bare before hook defaults to example scope, so one-time setup runs per example; the docs list the :suite/:context/:example ordering to make the intended scope explicit.

variants.name: Minitest::Test with setup and assert_equal
variants.implementation_notes: Minitest ships with Ruby and stays close to the language: subclass Minitest::Test, put the arrange beat in setup, name methods test_*, and assert with assert_equal or refute_match; minitest/spec layers describe/it vocabulary over the same engine, so the style choice is presentation, not structure. Because the framework deliberately reinvents nothing from Ruby, the beats are plain methods and blocks with no DSL to learn.
variants.code_sketch:
class TestAccount < Minitest::Test
  def setup                              # Arrange
    @account = Account.new(balance: 100)
  end

  def test_withdraw_reduces_balance
    ok = @account.withdraw(30)           # Act
    assert ok                            # Assert
    assert_equal 70, @account.balance
  end
end
pitfalls: assert_equal(expected, actual) reports the operands in that order; swapping them still passes and reverses the diff in the failure output.
Parallel execution (parallelize_me! or MT_CPU) makes global state touched in setup a race, because setup runs per test against shared process state.
Raising an exception instead of using the assertion API reports the test as an error, not a failure, and the expectation is no longer named by the assertion.
